Kimi.content:
# Moonshot (Kimi)

Moonshot AI provides an OpenAI-compatible API for its Kimi models — the Kimi K3 and K2 thinking models and the Moonshot v1 generation models. The Moonshot provider extends the OpenAI provider, so all of its options are supported.

## Setup

- Get an API key from the Kimi (Moonshot) platform.
- Set theMOONSHOT_API_KEY environment variable or specify apiKey in your config.

Kimi K3 requires a successful account top-up of at least $1; see the access requirements.
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3

Bothmoonshot:<model> and moonshot:chat:<model> resolve to the chat completions endpoint. If you omit the model, the provider defaults to kimi-k3.

## Available Models

Moonshot's lineup rotates over time — call the list models API (GET https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/models) for the live set. As of writing:

- Kimi K3 — flagship thinking model, 1M context:kimi-k3 (released July 2026). Always-on reasoning, native image and video understanding, and a top-level reasoning_effort control (see below).
- Kimi K2 — thinking models, 256k context:kimi-k2.6, kimi-k2.5, kimi-k2.7-code, kimi-k2.7-code-highspeed. These reason before answering and emit a separate reasoning stream (see below).
- Moonshot v1 — legacy generation models:moonshot-v1-8k, moonshot-v1-32k, moonshot-v1-128k (context-length variants) and the vision variants moonshot-v1-8k-vision-preview / moonshot-v1-32k-vision-preview / moonshot-v1-128k-vision-preview; existing accounts may also see the auto-router moonshot-v1-auto in the list-models API. The moonshot-v1 series and kimi-k2.5 are closed to newly registered users and sunset platform-wide on August 31, 2026.

The olderkimi-k2-0711-preview, kimi-k2-0905-preview, kimi-k2-turbo-preview, kimi-k2-thinking, kimi-k2-thinking-turbo, and kimi-latest ids were discontinued in 2026 — Moonshot recommends migrating to kimi-k3.

## Configuration
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3 # flagship thinking model — leave sampling params unset
  - id: moonshot:moonshot-v1-8k # legacy generation model — accepts arbitrary sampling
    config:
      temperature: 0.2
      max_tokens: 1024

### Configuration Options

The provider accepts every option the OpenAI provider supports. Commonly used:

- temperature, max_tokens, top_p, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty
- stream
- response_format (JSON mode), tools / tool_choice (function calling)
- showThinking — set to false to drop a thinking model's reasoning from the graded output (default true)
- cost, inputCost, outputCost, cacheReadCost — Moonshot ships no built-in price table, so set these to track cost. Every override is in USD per token. Moonshot's official pricing page publishes rates in USD per 1 million tokens, so divide each published rate by 1,000,000 before configuring it. inputCost/outputCost take precedence over the flat cost; cacheReadCost prices cached prompt tokens.

For example, these illustrative per-million rates convert to per-token overrides. Check the official pricing page for the current rates for your model before using them.
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3
    config:
      inputCost: 0.000003 # $3.00 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      cacheReadCost: 0.0000003 # $0.30 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      outputCost: 0.000015 # $15.00 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k2.6
    config:
      inputCost: 0.00000095 # $0.95 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      cacheReadCost: 0.00000016 # $0.16 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000
      outputCost: 0.000004 # $4.00 per 1M tokens divided by 1,000,000

Any other parameter supported by the OpenAI provider is forwarded as-is.

## Kimi thinking models

Thekimi-k3 and kimi-k2.x models are reasoning models and behave differently from the moonshot-v1 family:

- Fixed sampling parameters. Kimi pinstemperature (1.0 with thinking on), top_p, n, and the penalties to fixed values and returns a 400 ("invalid temperature: only 1 is allowed for this model") for any other value. The provider therefore does not send promptfoo's default temperature/max_tokens for kimi-* models — leave them unset (recommended) or set temperature: 1. The moonshot-v1 models accept arbitrary sampling values.
- Reasoning output. Kimi returns a separatereasoning_content stream that promptfoo surfaces with a Thinking: … prefix. Set showThinking: false when you assert on structured output (for example is-json) so the reasoning doesn't contaminate the parsed result.
- Token budget. Reasoning tokens count against the output budget. When you leave the token limit unset the provider lets Moonshot apply its server default (32k for K2.x, 131k for K3); if you set one, leave generous headroom for the answer. Moonshot's canonical field ismax_completion_tokens (max_tokens is a deprecated alias) — the provider sends max_completion_tokens for kimi-* models whichever of the two you configure.
- Controlling thinking. The two generations use different, mutually exclusive controls:
- kimi-k3 is always thinking and accepts a top-level reasoning_effort field, which the provider forwards from config.reasoning_effort. Supported values are low, high, and max (the default). Do not send the K2.x thinking parameter to K3 — the API rejects it.
- kimi-k2.6 and kimi-k2.5 support thinking: { type: disabled } (pass it via config.passthrough); kimi-k2.7-code is always thinking. The thinking parameter is K2.x-only.
- Settingconfig.reasoning_effort on a non-K3 model is a configuration error and the provider fails fast with a clear message instead of sending it.

providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3
    config:
      showThinking: false
      reasoning_effort: max # optional: low, high, or max (default)
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k2.6
    config:
      passthrough:
        thinking: { type: disabled } # K2.x only: turn reasoning off

See the Kimi K3 quickstart and Using Thinking Models for the full behavior matrix.

## Vision

The vision models (moonshot-v1-*-vision-preview) and the multimodal Kimi models (kimi-k3, kimi-k2.5, kimi-k2.6, kimi-k2.7-code, kimi-k2.7-code-highspeed) accept base64-encoded image input using the standard OpenAI image_url content format. Moonshot does not accept remote image URLs — embed images as data: URIs or reference files uploaded to the Kimi platform as ms://<file-id>. Video input is supported by kimi-k3, kimi-k2.6, kimi-k2.7-code, and kimi-k2.7-code-highspeed, referenced the same way after uploading via the files API. See Use the Kimi Vision Model.

## Example Usage
providers:
  - id: moonshot:kimi-k3
  - id: openai:gpt-4o-mini

prompts:
  - 'Summarize the following in one sentence: {{text}}'

tests:
  - vars:
      text: 'Promptfoo is an open-source tool for testing and evaluating LLM apps.'

A runnable comparison lives in examples/provider-moonshot.

## API Details

- Base URL:https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 (global). China-mainland keys use https://api.moonshot.cn/v1 — point at it with apiBaseUrl, since the global and China platforms issue region-locked keys.
- OpenAI-compatible chat completions API.
- Full API documentation.

## See Also

- OpenAI Provider — compatible configuration options
- Kimi model list and pricing

Skip to main content

Kimi (Moonshot AI)

# Kimi-K2.6

## 1. Model Introduction
Kimi-K2.6 is an open-source, native multimodal agentic model by Moonshot AI, delivering industry-leading coding, long-horizon execution, and agent swarm capabilities. It matches or surpasses GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, and Gemini 3.1 Pro across key benchmarks. Key Features:
- Long-Horizon Coding: Excels at complex, end-to-end coding tasks with 13+ hours of continuous execution and 4,000+ lines of code modification, generalizing across languages (Rust, Go, Python) and tasks (frontend, devops, performance optimization).
- Coding-Driven Design: Transforms prompts and visual inputs into production-ready interfaces with motion-rich elements including WebGL shaders, GSAP + Framer Motion, and Three.js 3D.
- Agent Swarms Elevated: Scales to 300 parallel sub-agents executing 4,000 coordinated steps per run. One prompt, 100+ files.
- Proactive Agents: Powers OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and other autonomous frameworks for 5-day continuous operation.
- Native Multimodality: Pre-trained on vision–language tokens with MoonViT (400M parameters) for visual understanding, cross-modal reasoning, and agentic tool use grounded in visual inputs.

Benchmark | Score 
---|---
HLE w/ tools | 54.0 
SWE-Bench Pro | 58.6 
SWE-bench Multilingual | 76.7 
BrowseComp | 83.2 
Toolathlon | 50.0 
AIME 2026 | 96.4 
GPQA-Diamond | 90.5 
LiveCodeBench | 89.6 

Recommended Generation Parameters:
- Thinking Mode:temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95
- Instant Mode:temperature=0.6, top_p=0.95

- INT4 (native checkpoint): moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6
- NVFP4 (4-bit quantized, NVIDIA Blackwell): nvidia/Kimi-K2.6-NVFP4

## 2. SGLang Installation
Refer to the official SGLang installation guide.

## 3. Model Deployment

### 3.1 Basic Configuration
Interactive Command Generator: Use the configuration selector below to automatically generate the appropriate deployment command for your hardware platform, deployment strategy, and capabilities.
Hardware Platform

Quantization

Reasoning Parser

Tool Call Parser

DP Attention

Speculative Decoding

Run this Command:
sglang serve \
  --model-path moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6 \
  --tp 8 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --reasoning-parser kimi_k2 \
  --tool-call-parser kimi_k2 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 30000

### 3.2 Configuration Tips

- Memory: Requires GPUs with ≥140GB each. The native INT4 checkpoint supports H200 (8×, TP=8), B300 (8×, TP=8), GB300 (4×, TP=4), MI300X/MI325X (4×, TP=4), and MI350X/MI355X (4×, TP=4). Use--context-length 128000 to conserve memory.
- NVFP4: Usenvidia/Kimi-K2.6-NVFP4 with --quantization modelopt_fp4 on NVIDIA Blackwell. Use tp=8 on B300 and tp=4 on GB300.
- AMD GPU TP Constraint: On AMD GPUs, TP must be ≤ 4 (not 8). Kimi-K2.6 has 64 attention heads; the AITER MLA kernel requiresheads_per_gpu % 16 == 0. With TP=4, each GPU gets 16 heads (valid). With TP=8, each GPU gets 8 heads (invalid).
- AMD Docker Image: Uselmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.9-rocm700-mi35x for MI350X/MI355X and lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.9-rocm700-mi30x for MI300X/MI325X.
- DP Attention: Enable with--attn-dp-size <N> for production throughput. A common choice is to set --attn-dp-size equal to --tp, but this is not required.
- Reasoning Parser: Add--reasoning-parser kimi_k2 to separate thinking and content in model outputs.
- Tool Call Parser: Add--tool-call-parser kimi_k2 for structured tool calls.
- AMD FP8 KV Cache: On AMD platforms the generator adds--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 by default and sets --mem-fraction-static 0.8 to fit the INT4 weights plus KV cache. FP8 KV cache trades a small amount of accuracy for memory; omit the flag if you observe accuracy regressions on your workload.

## 4. Model Invocation

### 4.1 Basic Usage
See Basic API Usage.

### 4.2 Advanced Usage

#### 4.2.1 Multimodal (Vision + Text) Input
Kimi-K2.6 supports native multimodal input with images:
Output Example:

Example
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1",
    api_key="EMPTY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "image_url",
                    "image_url": {
                        "url": "https://ofasys-multimodal-wlcb-3-toshanghai.oss-accelerate.aliyuncs.com/wpf272043/keepme/image/receipt.png"
                    }
                },
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": "What is in this image? Describe it in detail."
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Output
This image shows a **paper receipt from Auntie Anne's**, the pretzel chain restaurant. Here's a detailed breakdown:

## Header
- At the top left is the Auntie Anne's logo (a pretzel with a halo)
- The store name "**Auntie Anne's**" is printed prominently at the top
- Some text below the store name appears blurred/redacted (likely store location, address, or transaction details)

## Purchase Details
- **Item**: CINNAMON SUGAR
- **Quantity & Price**: 1 × 17,000
- **Item Total**: 17,000

## Financial Summary
- **SUB TOTAL**: 17,000
- **GRAND TOTAL**: 17,000
- **CASH IDR**: 20,000 (customer paid 20,000 Indonesian Rupiah)
- **CHANGE DUE**: 3,000

## Physical Description
- The receipt is printed on white thermal paper
- Some information in the middle section and toward the bottom is intentionally blurred/obscured
- The paper appears slightly curved/wrinkled and is placed on a dark brown surface (likely a table or counter)

The transaction is in **Indonesian Rupiah (IDR)**, indicating this purchase was made at an Auntie Anne's location in Indonesia. The customer bought one Cinnamon Sugar pretzel for 17,000 IDR and received 3,000 IDR in change after paying with 20,000 IDR cash.

#### 4.2.2 Reasoning Output
Kimi-K2.6 supports both thinking mode (default) and instant mode. Thinking Mode (default) — reasoning content is automatically separated:
Instant Mode (thinking off) — disable thinking for faster responses:

Example
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://localhost:30000/v1",
    api_key="EMPTY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Which one is bigger, 9.11 or 9.9? Think carefully."}
    ]
)

print("====== Reasoning Content (Thinking Mode) ======")
print(response.choices[0].message.reasoning_content)
print("====== Response (Thinking Mode) ======")
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Output Example:

Example
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Which one is bigger, 9.11 or 9.9? Think carefully."}
    ],
    extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"thinking": False}}
)

print("====== Response (Instant Mode) ======")
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Output
====== Reasoning Content (Thinking Mode) ======
The user is asking which number is bigger: 9.11 or 9.9. This seems straightforward, but there's a viral internet debate about this due to decimal confusion.

Let me think carefully:
- 9.11 means 9 + 11/100 = 9.11
- 9.9 means 9 + 9/10 = 9.90

So 9.9 = 9.90, and 9.90 > 9.11 because 0.90 > 0.11.

The confusion often comes from people thinking of software versioning (where 9.11 comes after 9.9) or comparing the numbers after the decimal as whole numbers (11 vs 9, thinking 11 > 9).

So mathematically, 9.9 is clearly bigger. 9.9 - 9.11 = 0.79.

I should explain this clearly and address the common misconception.
====== Response (Thinking Mode) ======
Mathematically, **9.9 is bigger**.

Here's why:

**9.9 = 9.90**

When comparing decimals, you need to look at the same place values:
- 9.11 = 9 ones, 1 tenth, and 1 hundredth
- 9.9 = 9 ones, 9 tenths, and 0 hundredths (9.90)

Since **0.90 > 0.11**, it follows that **9.9 > 9.11**.

The difference is:
9.9 - 9.11 = 0.79

**Why people get confused:** Many mistakenly treat the decimals like whole numbers (thinking "11 is bigger than 9") or confuse this with software version numbering (where version 9.11 comes after version 9.9). But in standard mathematics, 9.9 is definitively larger.
====== Response (Instant Mode) ======
I need to compare 9.11 and 9.9.

Let me think carefully by aligning the decimal places:

- 9.11 = 9 and 11/100 = 9.11

xAI.content:
#### Model Capabilities

# Best Practices Guide

This guide collects the practices that get the best results from Grok text and reasoning models on the xAI API. It covers which API to use, how to carry reasoning across turns, how to lower cost with prompt caching, how to configure requests, and how to run evaluations.

Start with these settings:

Setting | Recommendation 
---|---
API | Use the Responses API. Chat Completions is deprecated. 
Multi-turn history | Send the encrypted reasoning content back to the API with every turn. 
Prompt caching | Give each conversation its own prompt_cache_key, and only append to the conversation. 
Reasoning effort | Set it explicitly on every request, and record it with every result. 
Streaming and timeouts | Prefer streaming. Allow at least 900 seconds per request, and 1800 seconds or more for long-running evals. 
Output length | Set max_output_tokens above your longest expected answer, or leave it at its 128,000-token default. 
Sampling | Set temperature to 0.7 and top_p to 0.95, and don't stray far from them. 

## Use the Responses API

Use the Responses API (POST /v1/responses) with Grok reasoning models. The Chat Completions API is deprecated, and it has no field for the model's encrypted reasoning, so every multi-turn or tool-calling conversation sent through it discards the model's earlier thinking. New capabilities also arrive on the Responses API first.

If your code already uses Chat Completions, the comparison guide maps each parameter and response field to its Responses API equivalent.

Chat Completions is offered only as a legacy endpoint. Results from it understate what Grok reasoning models can do, especially across multiple turns and tool calls.

## Send encrypted reasoning back with every turn

Grok reasoning models think before they answer. The Responses API returns that reasoning as an encryptedreasoning item in the response's output array, alongside the message and any function calls. When you send these items back unchanged in the next request's input, the model stays aware of its earlier reasoning traces. This drastically improves performance on multi-turn conversations and agent loops, where each step builds on decisions the model already reasoned through.

There are two ways to keep reasoning in the conversation:

- Chain requests withprevious_response_id while store is on (the default). SpaceXAI stores the reasoning with the response and restores it for you.
- Manage the history yourself withstore: false. Request the reasoning with include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"] and append every output item to the next request's input. Each request is then self-contained and carries the full conversation, which you can log and replay.

grok-4.7 returns reasoning.encrypted_content on every Responses API response, whether or not include lists it. Your code still has to send it back. See Adding encrypted thinking content for the full reference.

The following loop runs a scripted multi-turn conversation. It streams each turn, carries the encrypted reasoning forward, reuses oneprompt_cache_key for the whole conversation, and prints how many input tokens were served from the cache:
import os
import uuid

import httpx
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.getenv("XAI_API_KEY"),
    base_url="https://api.x.ai/v1",
    timeout=httpx.Timeout(900.0),
)

conversation_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
history = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a careful analyst. Answer concisely."}]

turns = [
    "A train leaves at 9:40 and arrives at 13:05. How long is the trip?",
    "The return trip is 20% faster. When does it arrive if it leaves at 15:00?",
]

for turn in turns:
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": turn})
    stream = client.responses.create(
        model="grok-4.7",
        input=history,
        reasoning={"effort": "high"},
        temperature=0.7,
        top_p=0.95,
        include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
        store=False,
        stream=True,
        extra_body={"prompt_cache_key": conversation_id},
    )
    response = None
    for event in stream:
        if event.type == "response.output_text.delta":
            print(event.delta, end="", flush=True)
        elif event.type in ("response.completed", "response.incomplete"):
            response = event.response
    print()
    # Append every output item, including reasoning items with encrypted_content.
    history.extend(response.output)
    print(f"Cached tokens: {response.usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens}")
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({
    apiKey: process.env.XAI_API_KEY,
    baseURL: "https://api.x.ai/v1",
    timeout: 900000,
});

const conversationId = randomUUID();
const history = [
    { role: "system", content: "You are a careful analyst. Answer concisely." },
];

const turns = [
    "A train leaves at 9:40 and arrives at 13:05. How long is the trip?",
    "The return trip is 20% faster. When does it arrive if it leaves at 15:00?",
];

for (const turn of turns) {
    history.push({ role: "user", content: turn });
    const stream = await client.responses.create({
        model: "grok-4.7",
        input: history,
        reasoning: { effort: "high" },
        temperature: 0.7,
        top_p: 0.95,
        include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
        store: false,
        stream: true,
        prompt_cache_key: conversationId,
    });
    let response;
    for await (const event of stream) {
        if (event.type === "response.output_text.delta") {
            process.stdout.write(event.delta);
        } else if (event.type === "response.completed" || event.type === "response.incomplete") {
            response = event.response;
        }
    }
    console.log();
    // Append every output item, including reasoning items with encrypted_content.
    history.push(...response.output);
    console.log(`Cached tokens: ${response.usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens}`);
}
import os
import uuid

from xai_sdk import Client
from xai_sdk.chat import system, user

conversation_id = str(uuid.uuid4())

client = Client(
    api_key=os.getenv("XAI_API_KEY"),
    timeout=900,
    # Routes every turn of this conversation to the same server for cache reuse.
    metadata=(("x-grok-conv-id", conversation_id),),
)

chat = client.chat.create(
    model="grok-4.7",
    reasoning_effort="high",
    temperature=0.7,
    top_p=0.95,
    store_messages=False,
    use_encrypted_content=True,
)
chat.append(system("You are a careful analyst. Answer concisely."))

turns = [
    "A train leaves at 9:40 and arrives at 13:05. How long is the trip?",
    "The return trip is 20% faster. When does it arrive if it leaves at 15:00?",
]

for turn in turns:
    chat.append(user(turn))
    for response, chunk in chat.stream():
        print(chunk.content, end="", flush=True)
    print()
    # Appending the response also appends its encrypted reasoning.
    chat.append(response)
    print(f"Cached tokens: {response.usage.cached_prompt_text_tokens}")

The Vercel AI SDK carries encrypted reasoning automatically when you chain requests withpreviousResponseId; see Reasoning.

### Keep reasoning in agent loops

Tool-calling workloads need the same treatment. When the model calls a function, its reasoning item arrives in the sameoutput array as the function_call. Append the whole array, then your function_call_output items, so the model resumes with its plan intact when it reads the tool result:

Python (OpenAI)
import json

# client, tools, task_prompt, run_tool, and conversation_id come from your code.
def stream_turn(input_items):
    stream = client.responses.create(
        model="grok-4.7",
        input=input_items,
        tools=tools,
        reasoning={"effort": "high"},
        temperature=0.7,
        top_p=0.95,
        include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
        store=False,
        stream=True,
        extra_body={"prompt_cache_key": conversation_id},
    )
    for event in stream:
        if event.type in ("response.completed", "response.incomplete"):
            return event.response

input_items = [{"role": "user", "content": task_prompt}]

while True:
    response = stream_turn(input_items)
    # Reasoning, messages, and function calls all go back in order.
    input_items.extend(response.output)

    calls = [item for item in response.output if item.type == "function_call"]
    if not calls:
        break

    for call in calls:
        result = run_tool(call.name, json.loads(call.arguments))
        input_items.append({
            "type": "function_call_output",
            "call_id": call.call_id,
            "output": json.dumps(result),
        })

print(response.output_text)

Code drops reasoning most often in one of these ways:

- It extractsoutput_text and appends it as a plain assistant message, discarding the reasoning and function call items around it.
- It edits, reorders, or filters output items before sending them back. Pass them back exactly as received.
- It rebuilds the conversation from a transcript in a different format, such as a Chat Completionsmessages array, between turns.

For long agent loops, WebSocket mode reduces per-turn latency, and context compaction keeps long conversations within the context window.

## Use prompt caching to lower cost

The xAI API caches prompts automatically, and cached input tokens are billed at a lower rate than regular input tokens; see Pricing for each model's cached token price. The cache matches your input from the start: when a request begins with exactly the same items as an earlier request, that matching prefix is served from the cache, and only the new items are processed. Multi-turn conversations and agent loops benefit the most, because each turn resends everything before it.

To get the most cache hits:

- Give each conversation its ownprompt_cache_key and reuse it on every turn. Cache entries live on individual servers, and the k

## Speech to Speech

Build real-time, speech-to-speech voice agents over WebSockets, with low-latency turn-taking and tool use. For client-side apps, use Ephemeral Tokens to connect securely without exposing your API key.
import asyncio
import json
import os
import websockets

async def voice_agent():
    async with websockets.connect(
        "wss://api.x.ai/v1/realtime?model=grok-voice-latest",
        additional_headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['XAI_API_KEY']}"}
    ) as ws:
        # Configure voice and enable tools
        await ws.send(json.dumps({
            "type": "session.update",
            "session": {
                "voice": "eve",
                "instructions": "You are a helpful customer support agent.",
                "turn_detection": {"type": "server_vad"},
                "tools": [{"type": "web_search"}]
            }
        }))

        # Stream audio and receive responses
        async for message in ws:
            event = json.loads(message)
            if event["type"] == "response.output_audio.delta":
                # Play audio: base64.b64decode(event["delta"])
                pass

asyncio.run(voice_agent())

## Text to Speech

Convert text to spoken audio with a large roster of expressive voices. Inline speech tags (laughter, whispers, pauses) and output formats from high-fidelity MP3 to telephony μ-law. Unary requests or WebSocket streaming.

  }' \

Real World Examples: LiveKit · Pipecat

## Speech to Text

Transcribe audio files in a single call or stream over WebSocket. The default isgrok-voice-transcribe-2.0. 12 audio formats, word-level timestamps, multichannel, speaker diarization, Smart Turn end-of-turn detection, and 38+ languages.
curl -X POST https://api.x.ai/v1/stt \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $XAI_API_KEY" \
  -F model=grok-voice-transcribe-2.0 \
  -F file=@recording.mp3
import os
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.x.ai/v1/stt",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['XAI_API_KEY']}"},
    files={"file": ("recording.mp3", open("recording.mp3", "rb"), "audio/mpeg")},
    data={"model": "grok-voice-transcribe-2.0"},
)

print(response.json()["text"])
import fs from "fs";

const formData = new FormData();
formData.append("model", "grok-voice-transcribe-2.0");
formData.append("file", new Blob([fs.readFileSync("recording.mp3")]), "recording.mp3");

const response = await fetch("https://api.x.ai/v1/stt", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.XAI_API_KEY}` },
  body: formData,
});

const result = await response.json();
console.log(result.text);

Real World Examples: Voximplant

## Quick Start: Custom Voices

Clone a voice from a short reference clip, then use the resultingvoice_id anywhere a built-in voice works:
# 1. Create a custom voice from a reference audio clip (max 120s).
curl -X POST https://api.x.ai/v1/custom-voices \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $XAI_API_KEY" \
  -F "name=Friendly Narrator" \
  -F "language=en" \

  -d '{

    "voice_id": "nlbqfwie",
    "language": "en"
  }' \

with open("custom.mp3", "wb") as f:
    f.write(speech.content)

xAI.content:
# xAI (Grok)

Thexai provider supports xAI's Grok models through an API interface compatible with OpenAI's format, including text, vision, image generation, video generation, and voice workflows.

## Setup

To use xAI's API, set theXAI_API_KEY environment variable or specify via apiKey in the configuration file.
export XAI_API_KEY=your_api_key_here

When xAI is the selected fallback provider family, Promptfoo can use xAI defaults for grading, suggestions, synthesis, and web search. These automatic defaults currently usegrok-4.3 on the global endpoint; select grok-4.7, grok-4.6, or grok-4.5 explicitly where they are available. xAI does not currently expose a public embeddings or moderation API, so those defaults fall back to OpenAI when xAI is selected. Explicit provider IDs in your config still take precedence.

## Supported Models

The xAI provider includes support for the following model formats. xAI recommendsgrok-4.7 for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work; consult the public model catalog for current availability.

Legacy xAI model aliases

xAI periodically retires older model slugs and keeps them working through redirects. As of the May 15, 2026 (12:00 PM PT) retirement, requests to thegrok-4-1-fast, grok-4-fast, grok-4-0709, and grok-3 families redirect to grok-4.3 and use Grok 4.3 pricing. Requests to grok-code-fast-1 route to grok-build-0.1, while grok-imagine-image-pro routes to grok-imagine-image-quality. For new configs, use a current canonical model ID directly.

Regional model availability

xAI documents Grok 4.7 on its global and US regional endpoints, and announced Grok 4.5 availability in the EU API Console. Check your account before depending on Grok 4.7 in another region;grok-4.3 remains Promptfoo's automatic fallback.

### Grok 4.7 Models

- xai:grok-4.7 - Chat Completions; 500K context, text and image input, text output
- xai:responses:grok-4.7 - Responses API, including server-side tools and encrypted reasoning

Use the exactgrok-4.7 model ID. Grok 4.7 Fast is available in Cursor and Grok Build, but not on the public xAI API.

### Grok 4.6 Models

- xai:grok-4.6 - Previous flagship reasoning model for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work (500K context, text and image input)

xAI does not publish any aliases for this model, so target the exactgrok-4.6 id. There is no grok-4.6-latest.

### Grok 4.5 Models

- xai:grok-4.5 - Flagship reasoning model for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work (500K context, text and image input)
- xai:grok-4.5-latest - Alias for the Grok 4.5 family
- xai:grok-build-latest - Alias for the Grok 4.5 family

### Grok 4.3 Models

- xai:grok-4.3 - General-purpose reasoning model
- xai:grok-4.3-latest - Alias for the Grok 4.3 family
- xai:grok-latest - Alias for the Grok 4.3 family

### Grok 4.20 Models

- xai:grok-4.20-0309-reasoning - Reasoning model
- xai:grok-4.20 - Alias for the Grok 4.20 reasoning family
- xai:grok-4.20-reasoning - Alias for the Grok 4.20 reasoning family
- xai:grok-4.20-reasoning-latest - Alias for the Grok 4.20 reasoning family
- xai:grok-4.20-0309-non-reasoning - Non-reasoning variant
- xai:grok-4.20-non-reasoning - Alias for the Grok 4.20 non-reasoning family
- xai:grok-4.20-non-reasoning-latest - Alias for the Grok 4.20 non-reasoning family
- xai:grok-4.20-multi-agent-0309 - Multi-agent variant
- xai:grok-4.20-multi-agent - Alias for the Grok 4.20 multi-agent family
- xai:grok-4.20-multi-agent-latest - Alias for the Grok 4.20 multi-agent family

### Grok 4.1 Fast Models

These legacy IDs remain recognized for backward compatibility and redirect to Grok 4.3:

- xai:grok-4-1-fast-reasoning and its -latest aliases - Redirect with low reasoning effort
- xai:grok-4-1-fast-non-reasoning and its -latest aliases - Redirect with reasoning disabled

### Grok Code Fast Models

- xai:grok-build-0.1 - Canonical Grok Build coding model (256K context)
- xai:grok-code-fast-1 - Legacy alias that routes to grok-build-0.1
- xai:grok-code-fast - Alias for grok-build-0.1
- xai:grok-code-fast-1-0825 - Versioned alias for grok-build-0.1

### Grok-4 Fast Models

These legacy IDs remain recognized for backward compatibility and redirect to Grok 4.3:

- xai:grok-4-fast-reasoning and its aliases - Redirect with low reasoning effort
- xai:grok-4-fast-non-reasoning and its aliases - Redirect with reasoning disabled

### Grok-4 Models

- xai:grok-4-0709, xai:grok-4, and xai:grok-4-latest - Legacy IDs that redirect to Grok 4.3 with low reasoning effort

### Grok-3 Models

Thegrok-3, grok-3-beta, grok-3-fast, and related -latest IDs are legacy aliases that redirect to Grok 4.3. Promptfoo also recognizes the older Grok 3 Mini IDs for backward compatibility; verify their availability for your xAI account before relying on them.

### Grok-2 and previous Models

Promptfoo recognizes oldergrok-2, grok-beta, and vision IDs for existing configs, but they are not in xAI's current public catalog. Use a current model for new configs and verify legacy availability in the xAI Console.

## Configuration

The provider uses OpenAI-compatible configuration options plus Grok-specific options, subject to the model restrictions below. Example usage:

When xAI returnsusage.cost_in_usd_ticks, Promptfoo uses that exact billed amount, including cache discounts and request-level pricing adjustments. If ticks are unavailable, Promptfoo falls back to the model's catalog rates and applies the documented 2x premium when the response confirms service_tier: priority. Custom pricing can be set with cost, inputCost, outputCost, and cacheReadCost (all per-token rates); explicit overrides take precedence over reported ticks and are used as final rates without an additional priority multiplier.
providers:
  - id: xai:grok-4.7
    config:
      temperature: 0.7
      reasoning_effort: 'xhigh' # low, medium, high (default), or xhigh
      apiKey: your_api_key_here # Alternative to XAI_API_KEY

Bothxai:<model> Chat Completions and xai:responses:<model> support xAI
Priority Processing.
Set service_tier to priority for higher scheduling priority or default for standard
processing; omitting it also uses the default tier. Other OpenAI-compatible tier names are not
valid on xAI.

### Reasoning Support

Multiple Grok models support reasoning capabilities:

Grok 4.7 and 4.6: Chat requests can setreasoning_effort to low, medium, high (the default), or xhigh. Responses API requests use reasoning.effort. Reasoning cannot be disabled; Promptfoo rejects none locally.

For Grok 4.7, cap output withmax_completion_tokens for Chat Completions or max_output_tokens for Responses. Chat also accepts max_tokens as an alias; use one spelling throughout an eval, including defaults and test cases. Within test options, set a request option directly or under passthrough, not both. Reasoning effort accepts a direct eval variable such as {{ effort }}; see the optional Grok 4.7 providers in the xAI chat example.

Grok 4.5: Chat requests can setreasoning_effort to low, medium, or high (the default); Promptfoo rejects other values locally. Responses API requests use reasoning.effort with the same values.

Grok 4.3: General-purpose reasoning model. Chat requests can setreasoning_effort to none, low, medium, or high; Responses API requests use reasoning.effort.

Grok Code Fast Models: Thegrok-code-fast-1 family are reasoning models optimized for agentic coding workflows. They support:

- Function calling and tool usage
- Web search viasearch_parameters
- Fast inference with built-in reasoning

### Grok 4.7 Specific Behavior

The xAI release notes list $2/M input, $0.50/M cached input, and $6/M output. At 200K or more input tokens, the rates are $4/M, $1/M, and $12/M respectively. When the API does not return a billed cost, Promptfoo uses these rates, including the 10% premium on xAI's US endpoint; explicit custom rates still take precedence. As with other Grok 4 reasoning models, Promptfoo stripspresence_penalty, frequency_penalty, and stop.

The Responses API returns encrypted reasoning even wheninclude is omitted. Promptfoo keeps it in response.raw.output; pass these items back unchanged when managing conversation history yourself.

### Grok 4.5 Specific Behavior

Grok 4.5 is an earlier model for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work:

- 500K context window with text and image input
- Configurable reasoning:reasoning_effort accepts low, medium, or high (defaults to high); none is rejected
- Long-context pricing: requests with at least 200K input tokens use the higher catalog rate ($4/M input, $0.60/M cached input, and $12/M output instead of $2/M, $0.30/M, and $6/M); Promptfoo uses the exact billed ticks when xAI returns them
- Unsupported parameters:presence_penalty, frequency_penalty, and stop are rejected, and Promptfoo strips them automatically
- Ignored parameters: xAI silently ignoreslogprobs and top_logprobs on Grok 4.20 and newer models
- Server-side tools: usexai:responses:grok-4.5 for web search, X search, code execution, and MCP

providers:
  - id: xai:grok-4.5
    config:
      temperature: 0.7
      reasoning_effort: medium
      max_completion_tokens: 4096

### Grok 4.3 Specific Behavior

Grok 4.3 is a general-purpose alternative for text workflows:

- Responses API recommended: Usexai:responses:grok-4.3 for server-side tools, multi-turn state, and newer xAI capabilities
- Configurable reasoning: Setreasoning_effort to none, low, medium, or high
- Unsupported parameters: Same restrictions as other Grok 4-family reasoning models (presence_penalty, frequency_penalty, and stop)

providers:
  - id: xai:grok-4.3
    config:
      temperature: 0.7
      max_completion_tokens: 4096

Grok-3 Models: Promptfoo retains the legacy Grok 3 Mini reasoning-effort contract for backward compatibility. Use Grok 4.3 or Grok 4.7 for new configurations.

### Grok 4.1 Fast Specific Behavior

These retired IDs redirect to Grok 4.3 but retain their legacy request contract. Promptfoo stripsreasoning_effort, presence_penalty, freque

\# xAI \(Grok\)

Learn how to configure xAI Grok models for kagent\.

\#\# Configuring xAI \(Grok\)

xAI’s Grok models are OpenAI\-compatible\, so you can use the BYO OpenAI\-compatible provider configuration\.

\- Create a Kubernetes Secret that stores the API key\, replace\<your\_api\_key\> with an actual xAI API key\:

export XAI\_API\_KEY\=\<your\_api\_key\>
kubectl create secret generic kagent\-xai \-n kagent \-\-from\-literal XAI\_API\_KEY\=\$XAI\_API\_KEY

apiVersion\: kagent\.dev\/v1alpha2
kind\: ModelConfig
metadata\:

  namespace\: kagent
spec\:
  apiKeySecret\: kagent\-xai

  model\: grok\-3
  provider\: OpenAI
  openAI\:
    baseURL\: https\:\/\/api\.x\.ai\/v1
\- Apply the above resource to the cluster\.

Once the resource is applied\, you can select the model from the Model dropdown in the UI when creating or updating agents\.

cross_cutting.content:
# Cloudflare launches AI model that extracts information from emails, receipt photos in under 1 second

## AI Summary Cloudflare unveiled a preview version of its AI model, Cleric, that extracts information from documents and images quickly and at low cost, it said on its official blog on Oct. 19. The company said Cleric can be used on its Workers AI platform and will also be released in an open-weights form that anyone can download. Cleric extracts items such as names, dates and amounts and returns most answers within 1 second.

- Writer Chi-gyu Hwang
- published 2026-10-20 11:19:05

Cloudflare unveiled a preview version of its AI model, Cleric, that can extract information from documents and images quickly and at low cost, it said on its official blog on Oct. 19.

The company said Cleric can be used on Cloudflare's AI platform, Workers AI. Cloudflare plans to soon release it in an open-weights form that anyone can download and use.

Cleric is a "System 1"-type model. System 1 is a concept drawn from Daniel Kahneman's book "Thinking, Fast and Slow" and refers to models that make quick and accurate judgments. Large language models, or LLMs, that reason deeply and write text correspond to "System 2."

Cleric extracts names, dates and amounts from unstructured materials such as emails and photos of receipts. It also calculates or estimates values that are not in the material and predicts figures that may come next.

It does not generate text one character at a time like an LLM and instead produces an answer in one shot. Charges apply only to input data, and most answers come within 1 second. If it cannot find an answer, it does not fabricate a plausible value and marks it as "none." It also provides a confidence score with each answer.

For example, if a customer complaint email lists a product price of $649 and tax of $52.1, Cleric adds them and returns a total payment amount of $701.1. It also calculates elapsed days by comparing a delivery date with the email's 작성 date.

Cloudflare tested a method in which a decision model, Cleft, takes the values extracted by Cleric to make a determination, and an LLM writes the reply. The company said the method was 3.2 times faster and cost 49 percent less than a method that left every step to the LLM GLM-5.3.

Cloudflare acknowledged, however, that it is still weak at calculations that involve multiple steps. It added that it cannot properly estimate values without a basis and that its time-series forecasting is at a basic level.

About the Author

cross_cutting.content:
# Krafton unveils 30B-class LLM 'Raon-1 Mini' to boost cost efficiency

## AI Summary Krafton unveiled a preview version of its self-developed 30B-class large language model, Raon-1 Mini, on Oct. 21. The model supports Korean and English and was released on Hugging Face ahead of an official launch under an Apache 2.0 license. Krafton said the model uses a mixture-of-experts structure and its own linear attention technology to improve response speed and inference cost efficiency.

- Writer Hojeong Lee
- published 2026-10-21 14:23:46

Share this article

Krafton on Oct. 21 unveiled a preview version of its self-developed 30B-class large language model (LLM), Raon-1 Mini.

Raon-1 Mini is an LLM Krafton developed directly, from model design to training from scratch. It supports Korean and English, and was released in preview form on Hugging Face ahead of its official launch.

It applies the Apache 2.0 license. Anyone can download it for free and use it not only for research but also for commercial services and product development.

The model adopts a mixture-of-experts (MoE) structure that activates only 4 billion of its total 30 billion parameters as needed. Krafton combined this with its own linear attention technology, focusing on improving response speed and inference cost efficiency.

Krafton said its internal evaluations showed Raon-1 Mini recorded higher performance than overseas models of a similar scale, and approached domestic large models on some metrics. It highlighted Korean-language dialogue, instruction following and response speed as key strengths.

Its instruction-following capabilities extend beyond format specification and persona settings to use as an AI agent handling multi-step tasks. Krafton said it used cost-to-performance in real usage environments as a key criterion, rather than simple benchmark scores, during development.

Raon-1 Mini also serves as the base LLM for Krafton's AI model brand Raon, launched in April. Earlier, Krafton released four models as open source: the speech language model Raon-Speech, the real-time voice conversation model Raon-SpeechChat, the text-to-speech conversion model Raon-OpenTTS and the vision encoder Raon-VisionEncoder.

Krafton plans to further improve Raon-1 Mini's performance and release an official version. At the official launch, it will also publish a technical report covering the training process and final performance.

Kangwook Lee (이강욱), Krafton's chief AI officer (CAIO), said, "Based on AI R&D capabilities accumulated for more than 5 years, we independently developed a competitive language model." He said, "Through an LLM that raises performance while lowering the cost burden, we will expand the scope of AI use across various industries."

Krafton's AI research organization has published 54 papers so far at major international AI conferences including NeurIPS, the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) and the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). It said 9 main-track papers were accepted at NeurIPS 2026 this year.

About the Author
 Hojeong Lee lhj@d-today.co.kr

cross_cutting.description: MiniMax launches M3.1 Flash model, says it cuts AI agent costs by 70% Chinese artificial intelligence developer MiniMax Group Inc. today released M3.1 Flash, a faster and cheaper update to the M3 large language model it launched in June.
cross_cutting.content:
AI

### MiniMax launches M3.1 Flash model, says it cuts AI agent costs by 70%

Chinese artificial intelligence developer MiniMax Group Inc. today released M3.1 Flash, a faster and cheaper update to the M3 large language model it launched in June.

The release takes aim at the cost of running AI agents, which often need dozens of model calls to finish a single job. MiniMax said Flash represents its “ongoing exploration of the balance between efficiency and capability.” Agentic tasks cost 70% less to run than on its previous model, the company said, and inference is close to three times as fast, with output at everyday peak topping 200 tokens per second.

Size has barely changed from M3. MiniMax’s developer guide for the preview release lists 428 billion parameters in all, and the launch post credits the extra speed to more aggressive sparsity at inference time. Reasoning stays on for every request, with developers choosing one of five effort levels from Low to Max. The model accepts text, image and video input, and prompts can run to 1 million tokens.

In MiniMax’s own testing, M3.1 Flash scored 61.7 on OSWorld V2, which tests how well a model can operate a computer, and the company said no Chinese model has done better. BankerToolBench, a banking workflow test, gave it 76.2.

For security work, MiniMax pointed to an 82% score on CyberGym. University of California at Berkeley researchers built that benchmark to test whether AI agents can reproduce real software vulnerabilities, and the company listed code auditing, penetration testing and malware analysis among the jobs M3.1 Flash can take on.

At a flat 15 cents per million input tokens, M3.1 Flash lines up directly against the V4.1-Flash model from Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co. Ltd., which charges the same rate off-peak. DeepSeek said over the weekend that its updated V4.1-Flash resolved 77% of tasks on the DeepSWE v1.1 software engineering test. M3.1 Flash managed 73.7%, and neither result has been checked independently.

MiniMax, which has traded in Hong Kong since a $619 million initial public offering in January, saw its shares fall after the original V4.1-Flash launched in September, Bloomberg reported.

The launch also settles who was behind Space Bunny, an anonymous model that turned up on OpenRouter Inc.’s model routing service in late September. Community testers soon linked it to MiniMax by probing its tokenizer, and the company confirmed today that Space Bunny was an early M3.1 Flash build. More than 200 trillion tokens went through it while its maker stayed unnamed, according to the launch post.

M3.1 Flash is available now through the MiniMax API, the company’s M Plan subscription and its MiniMax Code desktop app. Output costs 60 cents per million tokens and cached input 1.5 cents. The company said it will release the Flash weights later, and a more capable Pro model is also coming.

cross_cutting.content:
# Nvidia Launches Nemotron 3.5: 120B Model Hits PCs [2026]

Nvidia used October 15, 2026 to make its biggest open-model move since it started publishing Nemotron weights for enterprise use. The chipmaker released three new models under the Nemotron 3.5 name, and for the first time, the lineup is built to span everything from data-center agents down to a laptop sitting on someone’s desk. TechCrunch, SDxCentral, and Forkast News all covered the launch within days of each other, a sign that the story landed well outside Nvidia’s usual developer-conference audience.

The headline model, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, packs 120 billion parameters and targets specialized, always-on enterprise agents. Alongside it, Nvidia shipped two smaller “Bolt” models meant to run locally: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, which uses native 2-bit quantization to squeeze 74 billion parameters into 24GB of memory, and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an edge-focused model scheduled to follow on October 23. Nvidia says the full lineup runs across NVIDIA RTX Spark machines, DGX Spark, DGX Station, RTX PRO systems, GeForce RTX PCs, and Jetson edge devices.

·

## What Nvidia Actually Announced on October 15

According to TechCrunch’s reporting on the launch, Nvidia’s pitch is straightforward: give developers and enterprises an open-weight model for whatever hardware tier they already own, instead of forcing every workload through a single hosted API. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB went live on October 15, 2026, while Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB was scheduled for October 23. That staggered rollout is itself notable: Nvidia is treating the edge model as a distinct release with its own timeline rather than bundling all three into a single day of coverage.

Kari Briski, Vice President of Open Models and Software at Nvidia, framed the release as closing a gap in the company’s model lineup. “Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Briski said, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the announcement. That line matters because it signals Nvidia is no longer positioning Nemotron as a single flagship model competing head-to-head with the biggest closed models. It is positioning it as a ladder, with a rung for every piece of hardware Nvidia sells.

## Nemotron 3.5 Super VL: the 120 Billion Parameter Enterprise Model

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL sits at the top of the new lineup. Nvidia describes it in its own generative AI announcements as an open 120-billion-parameter model built for the fastest task completion and highest accuracy among specialized, always-on agents. “Today, we’re expanding our Nemotron family of open models with Nemotron 3.5 Super VL,” Nvidia said in its public announcement of the release, adding that the model brings “visual understanding, reasoning, and tool use together to help AI agents complete more work in less time.”

Advertisement

The “VL” in the name signals vision-language capability, meaning the model is designed to process images and documents alongside text, not just read and write plain language. That distinction matters for enterprise agents because a huge share of real business workflows, think invoice processing, support tickets with screenshots, or compliance documents, mix visual and textual information. A model that can only read text has to route those tasks to a separate vision system, adding latency and cost. Nvidia is betting that folding vision into the core agent model removes that extra hop.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is aimed squarely at systems built for heavier compute: Nvidia’s RTX PRO workstations, DGX Station, and DGX Spark. These are not consumer machines. They’re the kind of hardware enterprise IT teams buy specifically to run large models in-house rather than renting inference from a hyperscaler, which keeps sensitive data off third-party servers. That’s a real selling point for regulated industries like healthcare, finance, and government, where sending customer data to an external AI vendor can trigger a compliance review all by itself.

## Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B: Squeezing 74B Parameters Into 24GB

The second model in the release, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, is where the engineering story gets more interesting. At 74 billion parameters, this model would normally need far more than 24GB of memory to run. Nvidia gets around that with native 2-bit quantization, a technique that compresses each parameter down to roughly a quarter of its usual storage footprint while trying to preserve as much of the model’s reasoning ability as possible.

Quantization is not a new idea in AI, but doing it natively, meaning the model is trained and tuned with the 2-bit format in mind rather than being compressed as an afterthought, is a harder engineering problem. Models quantized after the fact tend to lose more quality than ones built around the constraint from the start. Nvidia’s framing suggests Bolt 74B-A9B was designed around the 24GB ceiling from day one, which is also why the number shows up directly in the model’s name rather than being a footnote in a spec sheet.

Twenty-four gigabytes is a deliberate number. It lines up with the memory available on a growing class of local AI hardware, including Nvidia’s own RTX Spark laptops and higher-end GeForce RTX desktop GPUs. Fitting a 74-billion-parameter model inside that envelope means developers can run a genuinely large reasoning model without shipping every request to a cloud API, which cuts both latency and the recurring cost of inference calls.

## Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: the Edge Model for Lightweight Agents

The third model, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, is scheduled to arrive October 23, roughly a week after the other two. Nvidia lists it as sized for 4GB of memory, putting it in range of edge devices and lightweight PCs that can’t spare the resources Bolt 74B-A9B needs. The intended use case leans toward fast, conversational agent interactions rather than deep multistep reasoning, the kind of workload where response speed matters more than squeezing out every point of accuracy.

Pairing a 4GB model with Nvidia’s Jetson line is the clearest signal of where Nvidia expects this model to land: robotics, embedded systems, and other physical-AI applications where compute and power budgets are tight. A model that fits in 4GB can realistically run on hardware that would choke trying to load even the quantized 74B Bolt variant, which opens the door to agents embedded directly in devices rather than phoning home to a server for every decision.

## The Nemotron 3.5 Lineup at a Glance

The table below breaks down what Nvidia actually shipped, based on the company’s own announcement and reporting from TechCrunch and Yahoo Finance.

Model | Parameters | Memory Target | Primary Hardware | Availability 
---|---|---|---|---
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL | 120 billion | Enterprise-scale deployment | RTX PRO, DGX Station, DGX Spark | October 15, 2026 
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B | 74 billion (native 2-bit) | 24GB | GeForce RTX PCs, RTX Spark laptops | October 15, 2026 
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B | Edge-optimized | 4GB | Jetson, RTX Spark laptops | October 23, 2026 (scheduled) 

Notice what’s missing from that table: pricing. Nvidia’s own source material did not specify product prices for any of the three models, and neither did the reporting that followed the launch. That’s consistent with how Nvidia has handled most of its open-weight releases, the models themselves are typically free to download and use, with Nvidia’s actual revenue coming from the hardware people run them on, not licensing fees for the weights.

## Where These Models Actually Run: From RTX Spark to Jetson

The hardware list Nvidia published alongside Nemotron 3.5 is unusually broad for a single model family: NVIDIA RTX Spark, DGX Spark, DGX Station, RTX PRO systems, standard RTX systems, and Jetson devices all get a mention. Stack that against the three models and a pattern falls out. Super VL is built for the DGX and RTX PRO tier, the heavier enterprise hardware. Bolt 74B-A9B is sized for RTX Spark laptops and GeForce RTX PCs, the prosumer and developer tier. Bolt E4B is aimed at Jetson and other constrained edge hardware.

Advertisement

That’s a meaningfully different approach from treating “the model” as one artifact and leaving memory optimization up to whoever downloads it. Nvidia is explicitly matching model size to hardware tier at launch, which also happens to map neatly onto Nvidia’s own product catalog. Every one of the named systems is something Nvidia sells or whose core silicon Nvidia makes. An open model that only runs well on Nvidia hardware is still, in a very real sense, a hardware sales pitch.

## Why Nvidia Is Giving Away Models It Could Sell as a Service

It’s worth asking why a company sitting on the most valuable AI hardware franchise in the industry keeps releasing open-weight models instead of locking that capability behind a metered API the way OpenAI and Anthropic do. The answer traces back to how Nvidia actually makes money. Nvidia’s business is chips, and chips sell better when there’s a reason to own more of them. An open model that runs beautifully on Nvidia silicon and noticeably worse, or not at all, on anything else, gives enterprise buyers a direct incentive to standardize their AI infrastructure around Nvidia hardware rather than a mix of vendors.

There’s also a developer-ecosystem argument. Open weights mean researchers and startups can fine-tune, inspect, and redistribute the models, which tends to produce a wider base of tools, integrations, and bug reports than a closed API ever generates on its own. That ecosystem effect compounds: more developers building on Nemotron

cross_cutting.content:
# Pax8 Launches 8os, the First Agentic Workforce Operating System for Partners and Their Small Business Customers

COPENHAGEN, DENMARK (October 19, 2026) – Pax8, the global AI and cloud Marketplace for small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), today announced Pax8’s 8os and 8bot at its annual Beyond EMEA conference in Copenhagen, Denmark. 8os is the first operating system for the agentic workforce, providing managed intelligence providers (MIPs) with a single place to govern the fragmented AI landscape across every SMB customer they serve. Built on a proven commerce foundation, 8os enables partners to operationalize their managed intelligence services and deliver business outcomes to their customers at predictable costs. Through 8os, partners can deploy and manage a diverse agentic workforce, including 8bot, Pax8’s packaged, managed AI coworker that helps client employees move everyday work forward. Together, 8os and 8bot give MIPs a way to govern and deploy AI centrally while bringing its value directly to the people and businesses they serve.

The Problem: Expanding and Ungoverned AI Is Already Inside Small Businesses Without an Operating System

AI is already operating inside small businesses, and the vast majority see it as a competitive advantage. But in a market with a rapidly growing number of vendors and offerings, AI is largely without oversight, creating agent sprawl and security risks that undermine that advantage. According to the Pax8 SMB AI Pulse Reports, 90% of SMBs are using or experimenting with AI, yet just 23% have a documented AI use policy, and nearly half of SMBs are finding shadow AI in the business. Until now, governance and cost-tracking tools have been widely unavailable.

The challenge is no longer simply adopting AI. It is managing the work it does. As tools and agents multiply, work and context become fragmented, costs and risks become harder to track, and businesses lack a unified way to govern AI and translate isolated productivity gains into consistent business outcomes.

Adoption and building outpaces processes: 71% of SMBs using AI have already built at least one AI solution, but only 31% of those builders have a formal review or approval process.

Increased fragmentation and shadow AI in the SMB: The recent proliferation of agentic solutions is driving an increasingly fractured array of agents and bots in businesses. Making operations and governance even more challenging, 47% say they’ve discovered some form of unsanctioned “shadow AI” inside their business in just the past six months, highlighting existing risks inside these businesses.

Looking for trusted intelligence providers: 65% of small business leaders believe they need to move fast on AI, and 84% say they would trust an outside technology advisor to help implement it. Additionally, 70% agree they need outside partners to fully realize the technology’s value. 8os closes that gap by helping the MIP deliver AI value safely and effectively to their SMB clients.

Introducing 8os: The Operating System for the Agentic Workforce, Built for MIPs

“AI is becoming a worker, and that changes what small businesses need from their technology partners,” said Scott Chasin, CEO of Pax8. “The agentic workforce will be diverse. It will span different agents, models, tools, and providers, and all that intelligence has to be governed, managed, and turned into real business outcomes. That’s what we built 8os and 8bot to do. 8os gives our partners the operating system to manage that complexity across every customer, while 8bot gives them a managed AI coworker they can deploy, support, and monetize. Together, they make managed intelligence repeatable and scalable. This is the next chapter of the small business economy, and our partners are built to lead it.”

8os was developed to make managed intelligence structured and repeatable for partners. Built on Pax8’s existing multi-tenant, commerce, identity, and billing infrastructure, 8os delivers three things:

One governed agentic workforce: Different agents, models, tools, and providers become one workforce under partner control with clear ownership, shared operating rules, and accountability across every client they serve.

Compounding intelligence: Client-specific memory and context help AI workers deliver more relevant work over time.

Predictable economics: Usage and cost are tracked per user and per customer, hard caps stop runaway bills, and the MIP sets the price with a simplified billing experience through the Pax8 relationship.

Unveiling 8bot: A Managed AI Coworker for Every Client Employee

8bot brings the value of the agentic workforce directly to SMB employees, providing an AI coworker that returns results employees and teams can review, refine, and use across the business. Operating within the governed environment of 8os, it helps MIPs make AI practical for employees and manageable as a resalable service across their small-business clients.

Packaged employee capacity: A ready-to-deploy offering designed for fast time-to-value, helping clients add employee capacity while giving partners a service they can deploy and start earning recurring revenue in minutes.

Governed by design: AI delivered through the client’s trusted technology relationship, with the partner managing deployment, governing its use, and supporting the service through 8os.

Value delivered at scale: A repeatable service model partners can extend across client employees, turning individual adoption into a broader managed intelligence opportunity.

“Our partners have told us they want to deliver AI value without building a custom solution for every client,” said Libby McIlhany, Chief Product Officer at Pax8. “We built 8os and 8bot with the partner experience in mind, giving them an effective way to manage and govern the AI running inside their customers’ businesses and a pre-packaged AI coworker that’s easy to deploy. Through these solutions, they can deliver measurable outcomes to SMBs globally and turn AI into a managed recurring service at scale.”

Starting this week, Pax8 is providing limited early access to 8os and 8bot, with general availability planned for early next year.

Visit the 8os and 8bot product pages to learn more.

About Pax8

Pax8 is the global AI and cloud Marketplace for small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs). Pax8 connects service providers and technology companies on a unified platform to discover, buy, sell, deploy, and manage technology solutions for SMBs. More than 47,000 IT partners and 800,000 SMBs rely on Pax8 for expertise, automation, and real-time insights to stay productive, protected, and prepared for the AI economy. Learn more at pax8.com.

# Optro launches domain-trained AI agents for audit and GRC

Optro has announced the launch of an expanded set of autonomous agentic products to empower risk teams across the enterprise. Unveiled at CRX (formerly Audit & Beyond), Optro’s annual user conference, the announcement marks the formal arrival of GRC Intelligence, the next evolution of GRC: a trusted system of record, agentic AI that acts on that data, and governance over all the AI operating within the enterprise.

Optro’s GRC Intelligence Platform is grounded in domain-trained precision, human-led control, and responsible governance. Rather than adapting generic AI models, Optro is the only GRC Intelligence Platform that delivers purpose-built GRC capabilities that operate strictly within team-defined guardrails and risk appetites. Every agent action, decision, model entry, and evidence trail is fully logged, cited, and audit-ready to ensure total enterprise confidence.

“Every risk leader is asking two questions: what are your AI agents standing on, and how are you governing the AI running across your enterprise?” said Happy Wang, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Optro. “We built both into one platform with intention. Our agents work inside your live, permissioned context, taking on real-world workflows to deliver the exact business outcomes you need—so teams can move fast with a human in control. We don’t just claim quality, we evidence it: from verifiable execution that yields high-value results, to thousands of tests before any release, and continuous monitoring once agents are live in your own environment, so your data stays with you. That is GRC Intelligence.”

Agentic capabilities announced today include:

- Autonomous testing: Optro’s leading agentic testing engine now extends beyond SOX to operational audit testing across all control types, delivering full population coverage via Optro Analytics and giving auditors time back for judgment-based strategic work. Upcoming platform enhancements will soon introduce automated evidence collection to further streamline audit workflows. In its first three months using Autonomous Testing, Reddit’s internal audit team automated 175 controls, more than 40 percent of its SOX scope, reducing testing time per control by 60 percent on average. The team has since expanded agentic testing to over 75 percent of its SOX controls and to other recurring testing programmes.
- Agentic stakeholder management: Reduces evidence follow-up by helping preparers clarify requests and address gaps before submission, so auditors spend less time chasing evidence and get to testing faster.
- Agentic risk assessment scoring: Analyses selected Optro data and recommends starting scores with supporting evidence. Audit teams spend less time on manual analysis and gain a faster, more consistent view of risk for planning and prioritisation.
- Agentic compliance: Turns compliance into a continuous programme, where AI agents run framework scoping, evidence collection, and control evaluation across every framework, while teams make judgments and own every attestation.
- Agentic TPRM: Delivers a prescriptive vendor assessment workflow where AI agents perform onboarding and due diligence tasks while teams configure policy and evaluate outcomes.
- Agentic AI governance: Automated intake pre-populates AI system records from existing documentation, and the evidence evaluator flags which controls are already satisfied. In addition, AI Discovery, previewing ahead of 2027 availability, surfaces shadow AI enterprise-wide.

GRC was built for an era where the process of managing risk was predictable: document it, mitigate it, move on. Those days are over. The world now demands that GRC tell you what happens next. Optro’s GRC Intelligence platform addresses this by building a system of action using autonomous AI agents to execute end-to-end workflows in real time.

# Nutanix launches MCP server to bring agentic AI to hybrid cloud operations

By Staff Writer on Oct 20, 2026 10:30AM

## In summary

- Nutanix has launched an open-source MCP server for Nutanix Cloud Platform, letting AI agents and developer tools automate hybrid multicloud operations securely.
- The server connects tools such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code and Cursor to NCP infrastructure via the Prism v4 API while enforcing existing security policies.
- Architectural features include role-based access control, traffic throttling against agent swarm attacks, audit logging and human-in-the-loop oversight for long-running tasks.

Nutanix has launched a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for its Nutanix Cloud Platform (NCP), giving enterprises a secure way to use AI agents and developer tools to automate hybrid multicloud operations.

The open-source software implements the MCP specification and connects AI tools - including GitHub Copilot, Claude Code and Cursor - to NCP infrastructure through the Nutanix Prism v4 API. It translates plain-English requests into API actions while automatically enforcing existing corporate security and access policies.

Key architectural features include role-based access control that confines agents to APIs for which they have explicit authorisation, built-in traffic throttling to prevent agent swarm attacks, comprehensive audit logging, and asynchronous task management for long-running operations. A "human-in-the-loop" capability keeps operator oversight in place.

For developers, the server provides AI coding assistants with system blueprints up front, allowing automated generation of platform-ready scripts in Python, Go, Java, JavaScript, PowerShell and REST/JSON-compatible formats.

"By creating a secure gateway between AI tools and our platform, we are giving customers the confidence to safely use AI to operate and govern their hybrid multicloud environments," said Thomas Cornely, executive vice president of product management at Nutanix.

# Walmart welcomes AI agents as Anthropic launches its own

Published:

U.S. shopping giant Walmart on Wednesday unveiled tools allowing artificial intelligence agents such as Meta’s Muse to shop on behalf of its customers, taking the opposite approach to rival Amazon, which bars outside AI agents from its platform.

AI agents are programs that can carry out multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf -- such as searching for products, comparing prices and completing a purchase -- rather than only answering questions as chatbots do.

Tech companies including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta are investing heavily in agents, which much of the industry sees as the next phase of the AI boom that followed the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022.

Anthropic on Wednesday released a preview of Claude Duet, an agent that works in the background across users’ connected apps and can make online purchases with their approval.

Its archrival OpenAI launched its own always-on agents, called Dots, last month.

Muse, which Meta launched in September and has made available only in the United States and Canada, has been downloaded more than 10 million times, according to an analysis of third-party data by Sensor Tower.

Walmart said it would launch “Agent Profiles” within the next month, letting customers register each AI assistant they use as a separate profile within their Walmart account so that purchases made by the agent appear apart from their own.

Customers will be able to require approval for every purchase or let an agent buy on its own up to a spending limit they set, such as $50, $100 or $200, and delete a profile at any time.

Walmart compared the arrangement to adding an authorized user to a credit card.

Amazon, the largest U.S. online retailer, has taken a harder line, blocking third-party shopping agents while promoting its own AI tools such as Alexa for Shopping and its Buy for Me feature.

Last month, Amazon blocked Muse from its site, with users shown a notice saying unauthorized AI agents violate Amazon’s conditions of use.

Amazon sued Perplexity in November 2025, accusing the startup of using its Comet browser agent to covertly make purchases on its marketplace, and has also moved to restrict agents from Google and OpenAI.

# Amex GBT launches agentic AI tool to accelerate hotel sourcing

American Express Global Business Travel (Amex GBT) has launched Hotel Lobby, an agentic AI capability designed to automate data-intensive tasks in hotel sourcing and shorten procurement cycles. The tool combines AI-driven workflow automation with human oversight, with the company targeting improved negotiated savings, hotel programme compliance and year-round optimisation of corporate travel spending.

American Express Global Business Travel (Amex GBT) has launched Hotel Lobby, an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) capability within its hotel sourcing consulting service, aimed at shortening sourcing cycles and supporting year-round optimisation of corporate hotel programmes.

The tool uses specialised AI agents for coverage, negotiation and sourcing to automate time-intensive tasks, including data cleansing, target rate calculations and request for proposal (RFP) validation. The company said the system is designed to handle workflow execution rather than simply respond to user queries, allowing hotel sourcing consultants to focus on strategy, negotiations and exceptions.

Hotel Lobby draws on negotiated rate benchmarks across thousands of properties, supplier performance data from more than USD 5 billion in managed hotel spending, and compliance trends across Amex GBT’s client portfolio.The company said its existing hotel sourcing methodology delivers average savings of 28.8 per cent against the best available rate and a 96 per cent property response rate across more than 80,000 hotels sourced annually. Hotel Lobby applies AI automation to this process while retaining human oversight for key decisions.

“Hotel Lobby gives you the rigor of a full sourcing cycle and the speed to spend more time negotiating,” said Sara Andell, director of consulting strategy at Amex GBT. “Our AI agents now handle the data work, compress sourcing cycles, and free our consultants to focus on what actually drives savings, backed by rich proprietary travel data and years of consulting experience.”

Amex GBT said many corporate travel programmes continue to rely on a single annual hotel sourcing cycle, despite changes in room rates, demand and traveller behaviour throughout the year. This can lead to gaps in hotel coverage, reduced compliance with negotiated rates and missed savings between request-for-proposal rounds.By automating data preparation and reducing the time required to complete sourcing, Hotel Lobby is intended to help teams begin negotiations with more comprehensive information and complete the process faster. The capability also lays the groundwork for continuous monitoring of hotel programmes beyond the initial sourcing cycle.

Hotel Lobby follows the principles of trusted data, governance and transparency used in Amex GBT’s broader agent-to-agent architecture, which the company said is already deployed across its travel servicing and booking products. It is the first in a planned series of AI-powered upgrades to Amex GBT Consulting.The company also plans to integrate the new capabilities further with its reporting and intelligence tools to provide clients with a more connected view of travel programme performance.Research commissioned by Amex GBT and conducted by Forrester found that 3 per cent of surveyed organisations described travel as part of a fully orchestrated enterprise workflow. Meanwhile, 92 per cent of IT decision-makers surveyed agreed that AI would transform travel into continuously optimised systems.
